meta.names_note: Product was called FictionalCMS Hosting until a 2025 rebrand. Older reviews use that name.

claim.statement: Teams migrate an existing site to FictionalCMS Cloud in two weeks or less.
company_says: Homepage banner promises a live site in 14 days.
Migration service page describes a guided two-week program with a dedicated engineer.

icp.summary: Marketing teams at mid-market companies running high-traffic content sites.
details: Buyer: marketing leader; user: web and content teams
Media, higher education, and B2B SaaS case studies

core_messaging.promise: Ship content faster without waiting on developers.
core_messaging.tone_voice: Confident and aspirational, written for marketers rather than engineers. Leans on speed metaphors and avoids technical detail until the docs.

differentiators.statement: Only CMS host with edge-native rendering

tests.subject: Teams migrate an existing site in two weeks or less.

standard.validated: Three or more independent ICP-matched accounts report migrations completed in about two weeks.
standard.plausible_unconfirmed: Mixed or sparse accounts that meet neither bar.
standard.invalidated: Three or more independent accounts report typical migrations well past two weeks, or company docs describe a longer standard timeline.

tests.bottom_line: Mid-market teams report 6 to 12 week migrations, and the company's own onboarding guide plans for 8.
tests.reasoning: The onboarding guide schedules an eight-week migration, contradicting the homepage. Three independent reviews report 6 to 12 weeks. The one two-week account came from a single-page site outside the ICP.

evidence.finding: Onboarding guide lays out an eight-week standard migration plan.
Mid-market media company reports a ten-week migration with two re-platforming delays.
B2B SaaS web lead says migration took about three months.
University web team reports six weeks, calling the timeline 'optimistic'.
Small agency moved a single-page site in under two weeks.
evidence.notes: Outside the ICP. Logged, not weighted.

tests.subject: Will mid-market marketing teams enjoy using FictionalCMS Cloud?

standard.validated: Happy is the dominant pattern among ICP-matched customers.
standard.plausible_unconfirmed: Content is dominant, or no clear pattern.
standard.invalidated: Frustrated plus Angry outnumber Happy plus Content.

tests.bottom_line: Content is the dominant pattern: teams get the outcome but find the editor slow and developer-dependent.
tests.reasoning: Four of seven ICP-matched accounts are Content. They report faster sites but still route layout changes through developers, which undercuts the core promise.

evidence.finding: Marketing manager: site speed improved, but every new page template needs a developer ticket.
Content lead: traffic handling is excellent, editor is clunky.
Web director: fast, stable, easy for the team. Would buy again.
Digital marketing lead: reliable hosting, visual editor limited to preset blocks.
Marketing ops: likes the dashboard, but campaign pages still ship late.
Content strategist: dependable and fast once set up.
Web team lead: uptime is great, publishing workflow is painful.

tests.subject: Ship content faster without waiting on developers.

standard.validated: Three or more independent ICP accounts report publishing new pages and layouts without developer help.
standard.plausible_unconfirmed: Accounts confirm faster publishing for text edits only, or evidence is mixed.
standard.invalidated: Three or more independent ICP accounts report developer dependency for routine page creation, or docs require developers for it.

tests.bottom_line: Text edits are self-serve, but new pages and layouts still need developers.
tests.reasoning: Docs state new templates require a developer role. Three independent reviews describe developer tickets for routine campaign pages.

evidence.finding: Docs: creating page templates requires the Developer role.
Reviewer: every new template is a developer ticket.
Reviewer: campaign pages still ship late because of dev queue.
Reviewer: visual editor limited to preset blocks.
Commissioned study reports 40% faster publishing.
evidence.notes: Paid for by Fictional CMS Co. Counts as a company claim.

tests.subject: Only CMS host with edge-native rendering

standard.validated: Capability confirmed independently and no named competitor documents an equivalent.
standard.plausible_unconfirmed: Capability confirmed but uniqueness can't be established either way.
standard.invalidated: One or more competitors publicly document an equivalent capability.

tests.bottom_line: The capability is real, but two competitors document the same architecture.
tests.reasoning: The locked standard sets one documented competitor equivalent as sufficient. Two competitor docs describe edge rendering for CMS-hosted sites.

evidence.finding: Independent benchmark confirms edge rendering on FictionalCMS Cloud.
Competitor A docs describe edge rendering for hosted CMS sites.
Competitor B launch post announces edge-native rendering.
2023 trade press profile calls FictionalCMS the first edge-native host.
evidence.notes: First is not only. Predates both competitor launches.

tests.subject: 99.99% uptime SLA on every plan

standard.validated: Published SLA terms cover every plan at 99.99% and the public status history is consistent with it.
standard.plausible_unconfirmed: SLA terms confirm the number but status history is incomplete.
standard.invalidated: SLA terms exclude some plans, or status history shows sustained misses.

tests.bottom_line: SLA terms cover every plan, and twelve months of status history supports it.
tests.reasoning: The standard rests on published SLA terms plus status history, so two independent confirmations of the history meet it. No plan exclusions found.

evidence.finding: SLA document lists 99.99% for all plans with service credits.
Third-party uptime monitor shows 99.991% over twelve months.
Status page history shows two incidents under one hour each in the past year.
Forum thread reports a four-hour outage in 2024.

open_questions: Is the two-week migration claim tied to the paid migration service tier only? The homepage doesn't say.
D3 (built-in A/B testing) was not tested. Two reviews mention it requires a separate add-on.
